To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) BMI1 collaborates in vivo with H-RAS and promotes increased proliferation, invasion, and resistance to apoptosis, and (2) BMI1 induces fulminant metastasis in vivo through acceleration of proliferation and inhibition of cell death.
BMI1 collaboratively induces an aggressive phenotype in breast cancer, and that this phenotype includes brain metastases.
BMI1 cooperates with H-Ras to induce an aggressive breast cancer phenotype with brain metastases, and that BMI1 is an important therapeutic target for aggressive breast cancers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of novel molecular targets in breast cancer.
the molecular basis of breast cancer metastasis.
the role of BMI1 in the development of breast cancer, and in particular the development of brain metastases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the BMI1 gene is a target for the development of a novel therapy for aggressive breast cancers.
BMI1 collaborats with H-RAS in breast cancer and is a potential target for therapy.
BMI1 cooperates with H-Ras to induce an aggressive breast cancer phenotype with brain metastases.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
BMI1 is an important target for the diagnosis and treatment of breast cancer, particularly aggressive forms of breast cancer.
BMI1 collaboratively with H-RAS induces an aggressive and metastasizing breast cancer phenotype.
BMI1 collaborated with oncogenic H-RAS to increase tumorigenicity and metastatic potential in breast cancer cells in vitro and in xenografts.
The main takeaway from our work is that
BMI1 is a key player in the aggressive phenotype induced by H-RAS and that it can be targeted for the diagnosis and treatment of breast cancer patients with aggressive disease.
BMI1 is a key driver of breast cancer metastasis.
BMI1 is an important target for treatment of aggressive breast cancers, especially those associated with H-RAS mutation or amplification.
